sections.hypothesis: Buying a short, sharp fall measured by a fast RSI, in an uptrend, and selling at the first bounce beats holding the same coin at the same average exposure on Sharpe, after costs, on BTC or ETH daily.
sections.rationale: Who pays: short-term liquidity providers earn a premium for buying from forced or impatient sellers, and prices overshoot then partly recover (Jegadeesh 1990 and Lehmann 1990 on short-term reversal; Connors and Alvarez on RSI(2) for the S&P 500). The 9,000-backtest video (Luke's YouTube batch 2) found mean reversion the only family positive on average out of sample, and RSI reversion survived on 20 tickers; batch 3's G2 (Connors' RSI(10)) is the same idea. Against it, honestly: this is the dip-buying family. Kestrel's own buy-big-down-days (+21% vs +42% for BTC at the same exposure), Fear & Greed contrarian and extreme-fear tests all failed, and the entry bar names reversals as a rejected family. The video's evidence is mostly equities with an upward drift and is never compared with holding at the same exposure. Freezing this note is Luke's knowing override of the entry bar (2026-11-15). It differs from the failed tests in its trigger (a 2-10 day RSI rather than one day's fall or sentiment) and its exits (first bounce, not a fixed hold).
sections.rules: Daily bars, UTC, spot, long only, BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT separately. In cash: buy when RSI over rsi_bars closes is below rsi_below and the close is above its trend_days average (no filter when 0). Holding: sell at a close above the previous day's high (QS exit) when exit_rsi_above is 0, or at RSI above exit_rsi_above when set; and after max_days closes when set. Fills at the next open, costs from kestrel.toml, 330 USDT. Period 2018-01 to 2025-10, before the holdout. Three settings, each on both coins (6 runs): (a) RSI(2) < 10, 200-day filter, QS exit (A2/A4); (b) RSI(5) < 30, 200-day filter, QS exit (A1's base); (c) RSI(10) < 30, 200-day filter, sell at RSI(10) > 40 or after 10 days (G2).
sections.falsification: The full scorecard on each run. The idea fails if no setting passes every test on a coin. A single passing run among six is checked against the luck test (deflated Sharpe counts all six and every robustness neighbour) before it is called anything. Random entry (test 9) is n/a: this holds weights. If the trend filter makes trades too rare (under 30), test 6 fails; the filter isn't dropped to rescue it.
sections.parameters: rsi_bars 2-14, rsi_below 5-40, trend_days 0-365, exit_rsi_above 0-90, max_days 0-30. Only the three settings above. The robustness check moves each parameter of each (about 15 neighbours a setting). The scale-in (A1's second half) and the no-filter variants aren't run.
sections.costs: A trade lasts 1-10 days. RSI(2) < 10 above the 200-day fires perhaps 10-20 times a year on a coin, so 10-20 round trips a year at about 22 bps: 2-4% a year in costs, a large share of a few days' bounce. Trials: 6 runs plus about 90 robustness neighbours, a big addition to the count (193 now); the luck bar will rise for every later strategy.
